Manifesto.title: Because what we wear stays with us.
Manifesto.body: Wherever we live, whatever age we reach, denim stays part of daily life. Because it is worn for years and sits against the skin, we go back to the very process that makes the color and ask again. What is it made from? What impurities remain? Can the results be verified? Blugene began with these questions.

Impurity.title: Our standards reach beyond what you can see.
Impurity.body: What we do not compromise on is the standard by which impurities are checked and controlled. In the tests presented in the catalogue, aniline and N-methylaniline were not detected in the CutisBio bio indigo on which Blugene is built.
Impurity.context: Aniline and N-methylaniline are used as starting materials or intermediates in chemical synthesis routes, and they can remain as unreacted residues in the final indigo powder. A number of certification standards limit the permitted concentration of these substances in textile dyes and in finished products.
Impurity.chartTitle: Aniline and N-methylaniline analysis of commercial indigo dyes
Impurity.chartCaption: The nine commercial samples from catalogue p.5 Figure 2-2 and Table 2-3. The vertical axis is in mg/kg and starts at 0.

Science.title: Rewriting the DNA of indigo.
Science.body: CutisBio produces indigo using the biosynthetic pathways of microorganisms together with fermentation. We have brought bioengineering to the way a long-loved blue is made.
Science.metaphorNote: “Rewriting the DNA of indigo” is a brand metaphor. It does not mean that the indigo molecule itself carries genes; it means that indigo is made through the biosynthetic pathways of microorganisms and fermentation.
Science.diagramNote: This is a conceptual diagram. The actual process requires energy and process inputs, and the illustration is a simplified view of the path taken by the feedstock carbon.

steps.title: Renewable feedstock
steps.text: Renewable carbon from biomass such as corn is the starting point.

steps.title: Microbial fermentation
steps.text: Indigo is made by fermentation that draws on the biosynthetic pathways of microorganisms.

steps.title: Indigo recovery and product forms
steps.text: After recovery and purification, it is made into powder and digital printing ink.

steps.title: Fabric dyeing and printing
steps.text: It is applied to cotton, silk and cashmere dyeing and to digital printing.

Environment.title: Thinking of the wearer. And of how it is made.
Environment.body: An indigo that starts from renewable carbon. From the origin of the feedstock through to compositional analysis, we explain our approach with material you can verify.
Environment.carbonCardText: This is the share of the carbon in the product that comes from renewable feedstock. It is based on the measured value in catalogue p.3 Table 1-1 (pMC 97.73), and it is not indigo purity or a carbon emissions reduction rate.
Environment.scopeNote: Product-level life cycle assessment (LCA), water use, energy and carbon emissions data are not included in this catalogue. Environmental performance figures outside the verified scope are not shown on this site.
Environment.imageAlt: A conceptual value-chain image running from feedstock crops through fermentation equipment and blue fabric to a person wearing denim. These are not photographs of an actual CutisBio plant or staff.

Performance.title: Dyeability confirmed on real fabric.

Performance.honestNote: This does not mean superiority in every category. Lower grades are also recorded for some colorfastness to rubbing items, and they appear in the tables exactly as recorded.
Performance.additionalCaseBody: A separate dyeing evaluation photograph held in the archive. It is labelled in Japanese with 4, 6 and 8 dyeing cycles and with バイオ②-1 / 合成 (synthetic) / バイオ②-2.

Technology.metaDescription: An explanation of the four routes to indigo, production based on microbial fermentation, and the biobased carbon test results.
Technology.heroTitle: Four ways to make blue, and the one we chose.
Technology.heroBody: There is more than one way to obtain indigo. The catalogue presents four routes, and the CutisBio bio indigo on which Blugene is built follows the microbial route.
Technology.routesCaption: Catalogue p.2 Figure 1-1. Chemical routes are marked in red and biological routes in yellow.
Technology.routesAlt: Diagram of four indigo synthesis routes starting from crude oil, biomass and indigo plants (catalogue p.2)

routes.name: Chemical indigo
routes.text: Indigo is synthesized via aniline obtained from crude oil. The catalogue marks this as a chemical route.

routes.name: Hybrid indigo
routes.text: Indigo is made via anthranilic acid obtained from biomass. The feedstock is renewable, but the intermediate stage differs from the purely microbial route.

routes.name: Bio indigo (microbial)
routes.text: Microorganisms convert tryptophan obtained from biomass into indigo. CutisBio bio indigo follows this route.

routes.name: Natural indigo (plant-derived)
routes.text: The pigment is extracted from indigo plants. The catalogue notes cases among commercial plant-derived indigos that appear to contain chemical indigo.

Technology.routesNote: The anthranilic acid stage of the hybrid route differs from the tryptophan stage of the microbial route. We have not simplified the two routes into one.
Technology.carbonCaption: Catalogue p.2 Figure 1-2. A comparison of the carbon cycle in the chemical route (top) and the bio route (bottom).
Technology.carbonAlt: Conceptual diagram comparing the carbon cycle of the chemical route and the bio route (catalogue p.2)
Technology.carbonBody: The chemical route takes its carbon from non-renewable crude oil, and the bio route from renewable biomass. This difference is confirmed by the biobased carbon content test.
Technology.safetyBody: The catalogue addresses the working environment associated with handling hazardous chemicals. This site makes no quantitative claims about worker safety and goes no further than describing the difference in the substances handled.
Technology.safetyAlt: Illustration contrasting the handling of hazardous chemicals with the handling of non-hazardous materials (catalogue p.4)
Technology.impurityBody: Aniline and N-methylaniline are starting materials or intermediates in chemical synthesis routes, and they can remain as unreacted residues in the final indigo powder. Because of their toxicity and possible carcinogenicity, a number of certification standards limit the permitted concentration in textile dyes and in finished products.
Technology.conceptCaptionSafety: Catalogue p.4 Figure 2-1. An illustration contrasting the handling of hazardous and non-hazardous substances; it is not a photograph of an actual workplace.

Tech.title: Blugene, an indigo made by microbial fermentation
Tech.description: How the bio indigo of Blugene by CutisBio is made, and how it has been confirmed by testing.
Tech.intro: Blue denim is the most loved of fabrics. There is more than one way to make its color. CutisBio produces indigo using the biosynthetic pathways of microorganisms together with fermentation.
Tech.section1Text: Aniline and N-methylaniline are starting materials or intermediates for chemically synthesized indigo, and they can remain as unreacted residues in the final powder. Because of their toxicity and possible carcinogenicity, certification standards including ZDHC, OEKO-TEX and GOTS limit the permitted concentration of these substances in textile dyes and in finished products. That is why we analyze both substances for each product and publish the results together with the detection limit.
Tech.comparisonCaption: Catalogue p.4 describes these two substances as starting materials or intermediates in the chemical route to indigo, and notes that because they are toxic and potentially carcinogenic, several certification standards limit their permitted concentration in textile dyes and finished products.
Tech.section2Text: CutisBio uses a fermentation process that draws on the biosynthetic pathways of microorganisms to convert tryptophan obtained from biomass into indigo. Of the four indigo synthesis routes presented in the catalogue, this is the microbial route.
Tech.section3Text: In KATRI's ASTM D6866-24a Method B test, biobased carbon content was measured at 98% (pMC 97.73), and in KOTERI's KS K 0734 2019 test aniline and N-methylaniline were not detected (method detection limit 5 mg/kg). According to the catalogue, colorfastness is at a level comparable to plant and chemical indigo, and the grade for each item can be seen exactly as recorded in the tables on the data page.
Tech.certSectionText: These are the certificates included in the supplied catalogue. Each original can be viewed together with its certification body, certificate number, covered product and the validity period stated in the document.

faqList.question: What is Blugene?
faqList.answer: Blugene is the brand name of the bio indigo that CutisBio Co., Ltd. produces by microbial fermentation. In the catalogue and the certificates it is recorded under its original product name, “Bio Indigo Dye Powder (Microbial Fermentation)”.

faqList.question: What does “98% biobased carbon content” mean?
faqList.answer: It means that 98% of the carbon in the product comes from renewable feedstock. It is the result of KATRI's ASTM D6866-24a Method B (AMS) test (pMC 97.73, report SBED25-00000153-1, 2025-05-22), and it is not indigo purity or a carbon emissions reduction rate.

faqList.question: Does “aniline not detected” mean the content is 0?
faqList.answer: No. It means that in KOTERI's KS K 0734 2019 test the result was below the method detection limit of 5 mg/kg and so was not detected (report 2025-0604-1132-C03, 2025-06-10). It does not mean 0 ppm or the complete absence of the substance.

faqList.question: Can it be used on existing dyeing equipment as it is?
faqList.answer: The catalogue records comparable performance to plant and chemical indigo in the dyeing of cotton, silk and cashmere. Results can vary with the mill, the fabric and the process conditions, so we recommend confirming actual application with a fabric sample.

faqList.question: Which products do the certifications apply to?
faqList.answer: The product named on the certificates is “CB Bio Indigo Dye Powder”. The product list for OEKO-TEX ECO PASSPORT is in an enclosure to the certificate, so the scope cannot be determined from the catalogue alone. Digital printing ink and finished denim garments are not automatically certified.

Tech.structuresTitle: Chemical structures of aniline and N-methylaniline
Tech.structuresNote: Skeletal formulae drawn directly in code (SVG) from verified chemical structures. They were not produced with an image generation tool.
Tech.structureAnilineDesc: A skeletal formula showing a benzene ring with a single amino group (NH2).
Tech.structureNMethylanilineDesc: A skeletal formula showing a benzene ring bonded to a nitrogen that carries one hydrogen and a methyl group (CH3).
